chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
## The ISG Inflection

In the year ended March 31 2026, Lenovo crossed the threshold management had spent more than a decade trying to reach. The Infrastructure Solutions Group, built around IBM's x86 server business, delivered record full-year revenue of US$19.2 billion, up 32 per cent year on year, and reached full-year profitability, with operating profit improving by US$142 million to US$73 million. In the fourth quarter alone, ISG revenue rose 37 per cent to US$5.6 billion, operating profit reached US$202 million, the AI-server pipeline stood at US$21 billion, and customer AI deployments topped 5,800. [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

## Corporate Identity

Lenovo Group Limited traded in Hong Kong as **0992.HK** and in the US over-the-counter market as **LNVGY**. Its key operation centres were **Beijing** and **Morrisville, North Carolina**, and the company said in its FY2025/26 release that it served customers in 180 markets. Yang Yuanqing, who joined the group in 1989, was executive director from 1997 and held the combined roles of chairman and chief executive at the frozen snapshot date. [Corporate Information](https://investor.lenovo.com/en/about/corpinfo.php); [Our Leadership](https://www.lenovo.com/us/en/about/who-we-are/our-leadership/index.html); [Board of Directors](https://investor.lenovo.com/en/cg/directors.php)

The group reported through three business units. The **Intelligent Devices Group (IDG)** remained the largest by revenue, spanning ThinkPad, ThinkBook, Yoga, Legion, Motorola smartphones, tablets, workstations, and adjacent devices. The **Infrastructure Solutions Group (ISG)** comprised servers, storage, edge and software-defined infrastructure under the ThinkSystem and ThinkAgile families. The **Solutions and Services Group (SSG)** provided managed services, project and solutions work, and TruScale consumption offerings. All three businesses posted double-digit year-on-year revenue growth in FY2025/26. [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

## Heritage: Three Defining Acquisitions

Lenovo's modern shape still traced to three deals. On December 7 2004 it agreed to buy IBM's Personal Computing Division for total consideration of about US$1.75 billion, including cash, stock and assumed liabilities; IBM took an 18.9 per cent stake, and the transaction closed in May 2005. On September 29 2014 Lenovo and IBM said the x86 server transaction would begin closing effective October 1 2014, with a purchase price of about US$2.1 billion. On January 29 2014 Lenovo agreed to acquire Motorola Mobility from Google for approximately US$2.91 billion, and it completed that deal on October 30 2014. [IBM PC acquisition](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/lenovo-to-acquire-ibm-personal-computing-division/); [IBM x86 closing](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/lenovo-set-to-close-acquisition-ibms-x86-server-business/); [Motorola acquisition](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/lenovo-to-acquire-motorola-mobility-from-google/); [Motorola closing](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/lenovo-completes-full-acquisition-motorola-mobility-from-google/)

## Revenue Trajectory

The top line still described a U-shape across the 2020s, but the recovery had already become visible inside the frozen window. The pandemic-era PC surge pushed FY2022 revenue to US$71.6 billion; post-Covid correction then drove revenue down to US$56.9 billion in FY2024. What changed the story was the speed of the rebound: revenue recovered to US$69.1 billion in FY2025 and then rose again to a record US$83.1 billion in FY2026. [Five-Year Financial Summary](https://investor.lenovo.com/en/financial/five_year_summary.php); [Lenovo FY2024/25 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2024-25/); [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

| Fiscal Year (ending March) | Group Revenue |
|---|---|
| FY2022 | US$71.6B |
| FY2023 | US$61.9B |
| FY2024 | US$56.9B |
| FY2025 | US$69.1B |
| FY2026 | **US$83.1B** |

## ISG: The AI Server Engine

ISG's FY2025/26 progression was uneven quarter to quarter but unmistakable in direction. Q1 revenue rose 36 per cent year on year to US$4.3 billion; Q2 rose 24 per cent to US$4.1 billion; Q3 reached a then-record US$5.2 billion, up 31 per cent; and Q4 rose again to US$5.6 billion, up 37 per cent. By year-end Lenovo said annual server manufacturing capacity had surpassed 70,000 racks across AI, compute and storage systems, including more than 11,000 direct-liquid-cooled racks built for AI workloads. [Lenovo Q1 FY2025/26](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/q1-fy-2025-26/); [Lenovo Q2 FY2025/26](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/q2-fy-2025-26/); [Lenovo Q3 FY2025/26](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/q3-fy-2025-26/); [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

## IDG and SSG

The device and services businesses also turned in a stronger set of numbers than the earlier draft reflected. In the FY2025/26 fourth quarter, IDG revenue increased 24 per cent year on year to US$14.6 billion; global PC market share reached a fourth-quarter record of 24.4 per cent; and premium-PC shipment mix reached 50 per cent, with shipments up 29 per cent year on year. SSG grew fourth-quarter revenue 19 per cent to US$2.6 billion and, for the full year, passed the US$10 billion mark for the first time. Adjusted group net income rose 42 per cent year on year to US$2.0 billion, while AI-related revenue rose 105 per cent for the full year and accounted for 33 per cent of group revenue. [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

Yang used the May 22 2026 release to set a sharper public ambition than the dossier previously captured: Lenovo said it was confident in becoming a **US$100 billion** company within two years. [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

## Dossier Questions

The chapters that followed examined four structurally open questions. First, **ISG AI-server competitive position**: Lenovo's US$19.2 billion of FY2026 ISG revenue now had to be read against Dell's US$60.8 billion of fiscal-2026 ISG revenue, HPE's US$17.7 billion of fiscal-2025 server revenue, and Supermicro's US$22.0 billion of fiscal-2025 net sales. Second, **IDG PC-cycle durability**: whether AI-PC demand and enterprise refresh could extend FY2026 momentum without replaying a post-cycle hangover. Third, **SSG services scaling**: whether a business that had crossed US$10 billion of annual revenue could keep increasing recurring mix fast enough to matter for valuation. Fourth, **governance**: Lenovo remained controlled by Legend Holdings, with a North Carolina operating anchor and a Chinese founding lineage, a structure that still required separate analysis in a period of supply-chain decoupling. [Dell FY2026 results](https://investors.delltechnologies.com/news-releases/news-release-details/dell-technologies-delivers-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-fiscal-3); [HPE FY2025 results](https://investors.hpe.com/~/media/Files/H/HP-Enterprise-IR/documents/q4-2025/q4-2025-earnings-press-release.pdf); [Supermicro FY2025 results](https://ir.supermicro.com/news/news-details/2025/Supermicro-Announces-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Fiscal-Year-2025-Financial-Results/default.aspx); [Lenovo shareholding](https://investor.lenovo.com/en/ir/shareholding.php)

chapters.title: From 1984 Legend Holdings through IBM acquisitions and ISG scaling
chapters.body:
## A Borrowed Laboratory, Eleven Engineers, and Two Hundred Thousand Renminbi

In 1984, what became Lenovo began with funding of RMB200,000 from the Institute of Computing Technology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and a founding group of 11 researchers including Liu Chuanzhi. Legend Holdings later described the company as having been set up in a bungalow of less than 20 square metres; Lenovo's own history page described the same origin more simply as the start of a PC pioneer with just US$25,000 of initial capital. [Legend company introduction](https://www.legendholdings.com.cn/Introduction_en/index.aspx?nodeid=1043); [Legend founder page](https://www.legendholdings.com.cn/common_en/index.aspx?nodeid=1122); [Lenovo history](https://www.lenovo.com/us/en/about/who-we-are/history/)

The first commercially meaningful technical product was the Chinese character card introduced in 1986, which Lenovo's history page said enabled computers to process the Chinese language. That early localisation work mattered because it foreshadowed the operating pattern that later defined the company: take a global hardware architecture, adapt it quickly to local demand, then scale. [Lenovo history](https://www.lenovo.com/us/en/about/who-we-are/history/)
## Legend's Decade: 1989–2004

By 1989 the company had rebranded as Legend Holdings and entered PC manufacturing in its own right. It listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange in 1994, raising capital that funded the production scale needed to compete in a domestic market filling rapidly with multinational players. By 1997 Legend had overtaken international rivals to hold the top position in China's PC market — a share it defended through aggressive pricing, tight control of a domestic distribution network, and the ability to configure machines to Chinese buyer specifications faster than any offshore competitor could manage.

Yang Yuanqing joined Lenovo in 1989. Lenovo's leadership page said he later played a central role in the company's transformation, while an official company release said he was already leading the PC business by 1994 and that Lenovo had been China's best-selling PC brand since 1997. He became the dominant operating successor to Liu before assuming the chairmanship in April 2005. [Our Leadership](https://www.lenovo.com/us/en/about/who-we-are/our-leadership/index.html); [Lenovo company profile](https://investor.lenovo.com/en/about/profile.php); [Lenovo on Yang and Liu](https://www.legendholdings.com.cn/common_en/index.aspx?nodeid=1122)

## The IBM Deal: Acquiring a Global Identity

On December 7 2004, Lenovo and IBM announced that Lenovo would acquire IBM's Personal Computing Division for total consideration of approximately US$1.75 billion, consisting of cash, equity and assumed liabilities. IBM said it would hold 18.9 per cent of Lenovo after closing, and Lenovo's history page recorded the transaction as having closed in May 2005. [IBM PC acquisition](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/lenovo-to-acquire-ibm-personal-computing-division/); [Lenovo history](https://www.lenovo.com/us/en/about/who-we-are/history/)

The strategic logic was compressive in both directions. IBM had concluded that commodity PC economics were incompatible with the high-margin services and software model it was pursuing under Samuel Palmisano; it wanted to exit gracefully while preserving ThinkPad's commercial relationships. Lenovo needed a route past China's borders: its domestic dominance had a ceiling, and building an international sales force, supply chain, and brand from scratch would have taken a decade. Buying IBM's division delivered all three at once.

The transaction also delivered something less tangible: legitimacy. The ThinkPad was, by 2005, the preferred laptop of corporate IT departments from Frankfurt to Chicago. Acquiring it signalled that a Beijing-based company could steward a global technology brand — a proposition that remained contested in Western boardrooms and needed demonstrating through execution.

Lenovo adopted the dual-centre structure that still defined it at the frozen date, with key operation centres in Beijing and Morrisville, North Carolina. IBM executive Stephen Ward was named chief executive of the enlarged company at the time of the PC deal, while Lenovo's FAQ said the group had officially adopted the name "Lenovo Group Limited" on April 1 2004. [IBM PC acquisition](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/lenovo-to-acquire-ibm-personal-computing-division/); [Corporate Information](https://investor.lenovo.com/en/about/corpinfo.php); [Lenovo FAQ](https://investor.lenovo.com/en/ir/faq.php)

## The 2014 Double Bet

By 2014 Yang had diagnosed two adjacent white spaces. The first was the enterprise server market, where IBM was again willing to sell a division it considered peripheral to its cloud-and-services strategy. The second was smartphones, where a brand with existing carrier relationships could accelerate Lenovo's nascent mobile ambitions.

In January 2014 Lenovo announced it would acquire IBM's System x x86 server business for approximately $2.1 billion. The transaction closed in October 2014 and transferred IBM's rack and tower servers, blade systems, and related networking products — along with a roster of enterprise customers — into what Lenovo would eventually formalise as its Infrastructure Solutions Group. The acquisition gave Lenovo immediate scale in enterprise hardware and an installed base from which to compete against Dell and Hewlett-Packard Enterprise in the commercial data-centre market.

The same October, Lenovo completed a second deal: the acquisition of Motorola Mobility from Google for approximately $2.9 billion. Google had paid $12.5 billion for Motorola in 2012, principally for its patent portfolio; having extracted that value, it sold the handset operation to Lenovo at a fraction of the entry price. The transaction provided Motorola's brand recognition in North America and Latin America, a manufacturing footprint, and carrier relationships in markets where Lenovo's own smartphone brand had made little progress.

| Acquisition | Closed | Consideration | Strategic Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| IBM Personal Computing Division | May 2005 | ~$1.75B | Global PC scale, ThinkPad brand, commercial customer base |
| IBM System x (x86 servers) | Oct 2014 | ~$2.1B | Enterprise server entry; ISG foundation |
| Motorola Mobility (from Google) | Oct 2014 | ~$2.9B | Smartphone brand; North American and Latin American carrier access |

The Motorola integration proved more difficult than the IBM server transaction. Smartphone margins compressed industry-wide, Chinese competitors flooded emerging markets, and Lenovo never replicated in mobile the model that had succeeded in PCs. The brand was retained in key markets but never became a material profit contributor relative to its acquisition cost.

## ISG and the AI Server Pivot: 2020–2026

The x86 server acquisition compounded slowly and then abruptly. Through much of the late 2010s and early 2020s, ISG remained subscale against Dell Technologies and Hewlett Packard Enterprise and regularly operated below the profit profile management wanted. The AI infrastructure wave changed that timing. Lenovo's FY2024/25 results said ISG revenue grew 63 per cent year on year to a record US$14.5 billion and that the business broke even in the second half of the year; FY2025/26 then showed another step up to US$19.2 billion of revenue and full-year profitability. [Lenovo FY2024/25 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2024-25/); [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

Lenovo's fiscal year runs from April through March. The revenue line therefore described a full cycle and then a recovery:

| Fiscal Year (Apr-Mar) | Revenue (US$bn) |
|---|---|
| FY2022 | 71.6 |
| FY2023 | 61.9 |
| FY2024 | 56.9 |
| FY2025 | 69.1 |
| FY2026 | 83.1 |

[Five-Year Financial Summary](https://investor.lenovo.com/en/financial/five_year_summary.php)

By the frozen date, Yang could frame the AI-server business not as a hoped-for second act to the 2014 IBM deal but as a realised one. Lenovo's May 2026 release disclosed a US$21 billion AI-server pipeline, more than 5,800 customer AI deployments and annual manufacturing capacity above 70,000 racks, including more than 11,000 direct-liquid-cooled racks. The line from the 1984 CAS-funded start-up, through the IBM PC and System x acquisitions, to a global supplier of AI infrastructure had become visible in the numbers rather than just in the narrative. [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

chapters.title: IDG (PCs), ISG (AI servers), SSG (services)
chapters.body:
## Three Franchises, One Pivot

Lenovo's three-segment structure described the company's evolution more accurately than any single top-line number. IDG carried the commercial-PC and device franchise; ISG carried the server, storage and AI-infrastructure bet assembled from IBM's x86 assets; and SSG carried the higher-margin software, managed-services and TruScale layer that management had spent years building around the hardware base. By the frozen date, the group was no longer a roughly US$57 billion company waiting for a cycle turn. FY2025/26 revenue reached US$83.1 billion, including US$58.9 billion from IDG, US$19.2 billion from ISG and more than US$10 billion from SSG. [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

## IDG: The PC Franchise and Its Durability

The Intelligent Devices Group remained the largest segment by revenue and the segment most tied to the PC market cycle that Lenovo had ridden longer than any other single hardware maker. ThinkPad was the anchor brand, acquired in the 2005 IBM transaction that handed Lenovo a global sales force, North Carolina engineering campus, and enterprise customer roster.

In the years that followed, Lenovo broadened IDG beyond the ThinkPad's traditional corporate-IT heartland. ThinkBook addressed the upper tier of small-business and cost-conscious commercial buyers who needed reliability without the premium ThinkPad price point. Yoga became the consumer and prosumer convertible line — a thin, hinged form factor that competed directly with HP's Spectre and Dell's XPS. Legion carved out a position in gaming hardware, a segment whose gross margins and brand cachet differ substantially from the commodity Windows notebook market. Tablets and smart devices — Lenovo-branded Android slates, smart displays, and accessories — rounded out the portfolio, giving IDG exposure to the attach-rate economics of the broader personal computing ecosystem.

The cycle dynamics of the early 2020s tested IDG severely. The Covid-era demand surge that drove fiscal 2022 revenue to US$71.6 billion — across the whole company, with IDG carrying the bulk — reversed sharply as enterprise refresh cycles completed and consumer spending retrenched. Fiscal 2023 revenue fell to US$61.9 billion; fiscal 2024 fell further to US$56.9 billion. IDG was not immune, and global PC demand tracked the same compression. [Five-Year Financial Summary](https://investor.lenovo.com/en/financial/five_year_summary.php) The Windows 11 upgrade cycle, long anticipated as a volume catalyst, proved more gradual than some forecasts had projected, though AI-capable PC hardware — machines shipped with neural processing units capable of running on-device inference — began creating a genuine incremental refresh argument by fiscal 2025. Lenovo marketed this category under the "AI PC" banner, arguing that enterprise buyers would need to replace aging fleets to run next-generation productivity workloads locally. Whether that thesis drives a durable multi-year cycle or proves a marketing overlay on an otherwise gradual refresh remained an open question at the frozen snapshot date.

The Legion gaming franchise and the Yoga premium consumer line gave IDG pockets of higher average selling price that partially offset unit-volume pressure in the mass commercial market. Across the segment, Lenovo's scale — it has held the global PC market-share leadership position by units for an extended period — provides procurement leverage on memory, display panels, and battery cells that smaller peers cannot replicate.

## ISG: From x86 Heritage to AI Server Scale

The Infrastructure Solutions Group is where Lenovo's most consequential forward bet has been placed. ISG traces to the 2014 IBM x86 server acquisition that gave Lenovo ThinkSystem and ThinkAgile platforms, engineering teams in Raleigh and Stuttgart, and a global enterprise customer base.

The decade that followed was uneven. ISG competed in a server market dominated by Dell Technologies and Hewlett Packard Enterprise, both of which had larger direct-sales forces and deeper integration with the enterprise software ecosystem. ISG's operating margins lagged IDG's, and the segment periodically absorbed losses that the PC franchise was left to subsidise. Yang Yuanqing was publicly consistent in defending the investment horizon, framing ISG as the infrastructure layer that would eventually capture value from the same cloud and enterprise compute buildout driving hyperscaler capex.

The AI infrastructure cycle that accelerated through 2023 and into 2024-2025 validated that thesis in a way the prior decade had not. Demand for GPU-dense servers — machines populated with Nvidia H100, H200, and AMD Instinct accelerators rather than standard CPU cores — created a market segment where Lenovo's manufacturing scale, its relationships with the Taiwanese ODM supply chain, and its ThinkSystem platform architecture proved competitive. Lenovo configured and shipped AI server SKUs under the ThinkSystem SR series, integrating Nvidia GPU trays into standard rack form factors and working through hyperscaler procurement channels alongside the direct enterprise sales force. ThinkAgile, the hyperconverged infrastructure line built on VMware and later extended to accommodate Kubernetes-based workloads, addressed a different buyer — the enterprise architect managing private cloud infrastructure rather than the hyperscaler building out a training cluster.

By the frozen date, the better way to describe ISG was sequentially. In FY2024/25 Lenovo said the segment broke even in the second half of the year after revenue rose 63 per cent to US$14.5 billion. In FY2025/26 it then reached full-year profitability, with revenue up another 32 per cent to US$19.2 billion and operating profit of US$73 million. The segment still trailed Dell's ISG in scale and faced aggressive AI-server competition from HPE and Supermicro, but it had moved out of the investment-only phase and into one where profitability could be measured against disclosed results. [Lenovo FY2024/25 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2024-25/); [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/); [Dell FY2026 results](https://investors.delltechnologies.com/news-releases/news-release-details/dell-technologies-delivers-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-fiscal-3); [HPE FY2025 results](https://investors.hpe.com/~/media/Files/H/HP-Enterprise-IR/documents/q4-2025/q4-2025-earnings-press-release.pdf); [Supermicro FY2025 results](https://ir.supermicro.com/news/news-details/2025/Supermicro-Announces-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Fiscal-Year-2025-Financial-Results/default.aspx)

| Segment | Primary brands | AI exposure | Operating margin status (FY2026) |
|---|---|---|---|
| IDG (Intelligent Devices Group) | ThinkPad, ThinkBook, Yoga, Legion, Motorola | AI PCs, smartphones, workstations | Positive; scale leader |
| ISG (Infrastructure Solutions Group) | ThinkSystem, ThinkAgile | AI servers, liquid cooling, rack-scale systems | Full-year profitable |
| SSG (Solutions and Services Group) | TruScale, managed services, solutions | AI services, enterprise AI deployment | Highest-margin segment; >20% Q4 margin |

## SSG: The Margin Engine and the Subscription Thesis

The Solutions and Services Group is the smallest of the three segments by revenue but carries the highest operating margin profile — the arithmetic that explains why Yang Yuanqing and the investor relations narrative at [investor.lenovo.com](https://investor.lenovo.com) have consistently emphasised SSG's growth rate as a leading indicator of the company's structural improvement.

SSG encompasses software, project-based professional services, and — most strategically — TruScale, Lenovo's as-a-service subscription model that allows enterprise customers to consume IT infrastructure on a consumption or subscription basis rather than purchasing hardware outright. TruScale covers devices (laptops and workstations provisioned as a managed service), servers, and storage, and positions Lenovo as a managed-services provider rather than a hardware vendor. The model mirrors the device-as-a-service offerings that HP Inc and Dell have developed, and the IT infrastructure subscription offers that HPE has built through its GreenLake platform.

The appeal to enterprise finance directors is straightforward: capital expenditure converts to operating expenditure, refresh cycles become vendor-managed, and the customer acquires a service-level commitment alongside the physical equipment. The appeal to Lenovo is margin accretion — recurring contract revenue carries a structurally higher gross margin than hardware boxes shipped on one-time purchase orders — and stickiness, because a customer on a multi-year TruScale contract is less price-sensitive to any single hardware generation than a customer who rebids each refresh cycle.

SSG also encompassed Lenovo's AI solutions vertical, which packaged hardware, software and professional services into deployable private-AI and hybrid-AI environments. By Q1 FY2025/26, Lenovo said the faster-growing managed-services, as-a-service, projects and solutions categories had risen to 58 per cent of SSG revenue; by Q4 that mix had reached 62 per cent. In other words, the services layer was not simply following the hardware cycle. It was becoming a larger share of the segment in its own right. [Lenovo Q1 FY2025/26](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/q1-fy-2025-26/); [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

The three-segment structure thus forms an integrated flywheel in theory: IDG generates the volume and customer relationships; ISG provides the infrastructure layer increasingly demanded by AI workloads; SSG extracts recurring margin from both by wrapping hardware in services, subscriptions, and software. The degree to which that flywheel produces compound margin expansion rather than segment-by-segment trade-offs — ISG investment depressing overall returns even as SSG scales — remained the core question for analysts modelling Lenovo's medium-term earnings trajectory at the end of the frozen window.

chapters.title: Revenue trajectory, ISG margin progression, capital structure
chapters.body:
The financial story visible by May 23 2026 no longer turned on whether Lenovo had merely stopped shrinking. By then the company had already moved far beyond the FY2024 trough. Revenue fell from US$71.6 billion in FY2022 to US$56.9 billion in FY2024, then rebounded to US$69.1 billion in FY2025 and a record US$83.1 billion in FY2026. The more interesting question was what had driven the recovery: part ordinary PC normalisation, part a genuine re-weighting toward AI infrastructure and services. [Five-Year Financial Summary](https://investor.lenovo.com/en/financial/five_year_summary.php); [Lenovo FY2024/25 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2024-25/); [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

## From Peak to Recovery

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (US$bn) | YoY Change | Principal Driver |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY2022 (ended Mar 2022) | 71.6 | +21% | Covid-era PC supercycle peak |
| FY2023 (ended Mar 2023) | 61.9 | -13% | PC correction and channel destocking |
| FY2024 (ended Mar 2024) | 56.9 | -8% | Demand trough, elongated refresh cycles |
| FY2025 (ended Mar 2025) | 69.1 | +21% | Double-digit growth across all groups, ISG hypergrowth |
| FY2026 (ended Mar 2026) | 83.1 | +20% | Record year led by AI infrastructure and broad-based growth |

The FY2022 figure had been inflated by the release of pandemic-compressed enterprise demand and elevated consumer notebook purchases. The correction that followed was painful but unsurprising: channel inventory had been built against scarcity, corporate fleets had already been refreshed, and average selling prices normalised. FY2023 and FY2024 therefore looked like a compression story. [Five-Year Financial Summary](https://investor.lenovo.com/en/financial/five_year_summary.php)

What the earlier draft missed was that the rebound had already started before the frozen window closed. Lenovo's FY2024/25 results, released on May 22 2025, showed revenue up 21 per cent to US$69.1 billion, the group's second-highest annual revenue on record. One year later the FY2025/26 release showed another 20 per cent increase to US$83.1 billion and the first year in which group revenue surpassed US$80 billion. [Lenovo FY2024/25 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2024-25/); [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

## ISG: The Long March to Profitability

ISG remained the most important change in the financial mix. For most of the decade after the IBM x86 acquisition, the segment operated as a strategic investment: scale had been bought, but margin had not yet followed. The turning point came in stages, not all at once. In FY2024/25 Lenovo said ISG revenue rose 63 per cent year on year to a record US$14.5 billion and that the business broke even in the second half of the fiscal year. In FY2025/26 the segment then delivered record full-year revenue of US$19.2 billion, up another 32 per cent, and reached full-year profitability with operating profit of US$73 million. [Lenovo FY2024/25 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2024-25/); [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

| Fiscal Year | ISG Operating Status | Key Development |
|---|---|---|
| FY2022 | Operating loss | Post-acquisition scale without AI tailwind |
| FY2023 | Operating loss | Losses narrowed while AI configurations broadened |
| FY2024 | Operating loss | Demand improved, but full-year profitability remained elusive |
| FY2025 | Second-half breakeven | Revenue reached US$14.5B; AI server demand hypergrew |
| FY2026 | Full-year profit | Revenue reached US$19.2B; operating profit was US$73M |

The fourth-quarter FY2026 figures made clear why the economics had changed. ISG revenue reached US$5.6 billion, operating profit US$202 million, and the AI-server pipeline US$21 billion, while annual manufacturing capacity surpassed 70,000 racks. Lenovo was no longer asking investors to underwrite a hypothetical infrastructure option; it was reporting a scaled business whose profitability had finally appeared at full-year level. [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

## The Three-Segment P&L Architecture

Yang Yuanqing's three-segment design had become easier to see in the numbers. IDG remained the cash engine, delivering US$58.9 billion of FY2025/26 revenue, up 17 per cent year on year, with market leadership strengthened across PCs and adjacencies. ISG became the growth engine, and SSG the margin engine: in FY2024/25 SSG revenue reached US$8.5 billion with a 21.1 per cent operating margin; in FY2025/26 it surpassed US$10 billion of annual revenue and maintained fourth-quarter operating margin of 22.4 per cent, with 62 per cent of Q4 revenue coming from Managed Services and Project and Solutions. [Lenovo FY2024/25 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2024-25/); [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

This was the point the older draft had blurred. Lenovo did not simply return to its old device-only shape after the post-Covid slump. The FY2026 revenue base was structurally different from FY2022's: it carried more services content, more AI-server exposure, and a positive full-year contribution from ISG that had been missing for most of the prior decade. AI-related revenue doubled year on year in FY2025/26 and accounted for 33 per cent of group revenue for the year, evidence that the infrastructure and services layers were no longer peripheral. [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

## Capital Structure and Allocation

The balance sheet also moved materially. Lenovo's five-year summary showed total assets rising to US$57.1 billion and net assets to US$8.4 billion at March 31 2026, versus US$44.2 billion and US$6.7 billion respectively a year earlier. The company remained dividend-paying through the cycle: the board declared a final dividend of 30.5 HK cents per share for FY2024/25 and 33.7 HK cents per share for FY2025/26. [Five-Year Financial Summary](https://investor.lenovo.com/en/financial/five_year_summary.php); [Lenovo FY2024/25 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2024-25/); [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

Capital allocation priorities were clearer by the frozen date than they had been a year earlier. Lenovo continued to fund R&D, which rose 13 per cent year on year to US$2.3 billion in FY2024/25 and then a further 9 per cent in FY2025/26; it kept building ISG manufacturing and go-to-market capacity; and it kept expanding the higher-value services layer. The result was a company that had first survived a severe PC-cycle reset and then used the rebound to arrive at a different earnings mix altogether. [Lenovo FY2024/25 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2024-25/); [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

chapters.title: Multi-year trajectory through PC cycle and ISG inflection
chapters.body:
## From Covid peak to trough, and from trough to record

Lenovo's revenue arc over the review period ended up being a five-year, not a four-year, story. The group hit a pandemic-era high of US$71.6 billion in FY2022, fell to US$61.9 billion in FY2023 and US$56.9 billion in FY2024 as the PC correction ran its course, then recovered sharply to US$69.1 billion in FY2025 and US$83.1 billion in FY2026. What had initially looked like a long stabilisation phase turned out, by the frozen window, to have become a two-step rebound. [Five-Year Financial Summary](https://investor.lenovo.com/en/financial/five_year_summary.php); [Lenovo FY2024/25 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2024-25/); [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

The first part of that drawdown was familiar to anyone who had watched the PC industry before. Enterprise refresh programmes had been pulled forward during 2020 and 2021; consumer demand had been inflated by stay-at-home spending; and distributors had over-ordered against shortages. As those distortions unwound, Lenovo's Intelligent Devices Group absorbed the impact just as HP, Dell and Acer did. [Five-Year Financial Summary](https://investor.lenovo.com/en/financial/five_year_summary.php)

## Quarterly cadence: where the inflection became visible

The real shift in the earnings story arrived after FY2024, not before it. Lenovo's FY2024/25 release showed a broad rebound already under way: group revenue rose 21 per cent year on year to US$69.1 billion, all business groups posted double-digit growth, and non-PC revenue mix rose to 47 per cent. The quarter-by-quarter progression in FY2025/26 then confirmed that the improvement had legs. Q1 revenue rose 22 per cent year on year to US$18.8 billion; Q2 rose 15 per cent to US$20.5 billion; Q3 reached a then-record US$22.2 billion, up 18 per cent; and Q4 came in at US$21.6 billion, up 27 per cent. [Lenovo FY2024/25 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2024-25/); [Lenovo Q1 FY2025/26](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/q1-fy-2025-26/); [Lenovo Q2 FY2025/26](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/q2-fy-2025-26/); [Lenovo Q3 FY2025/26](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/q3-fy-2025-26/); [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

The PC narrative mattered, but it was no longer the whole company. Lenovo used the FY2025/26 quarterly releases to say that AI-PC penetration was rising, premium-PC mix was improving, and commercial demand remained supportive; by Q4, global PC market share had reached 24.4 per cent and premium-PC mix had risen to 50 per cent. That was material for IDG, but the more consequential earnings swing came from infrastructure. [Lenovo Q1 FY2025/26](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/q1-fy-2025-26/); [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

## ISG: the pivot that changed the revenue mix

ISG moved from thesis to evidence during the frozen window. In FY2024/25 Lenovo said ISG revenue rose 63 per cent to US$14.5 billion and the business broke even in the second half of the year. In FY2025/26 ISG then reported another 32 per cent of growth to US$19.2 billion, while full-year operating profit reached US$73 million. Quarterly revenue ran at US$4.3 billion in Q1, US$4.1 billion in Q2, US$5.2 billion in Q3 and US$5.6 billion in Q4; by year-end the AI-server pipeline stood at US$21 billion. [Lenovo FY2024/25 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2024-25/); [Lenovo Q1 FY2025/26](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/q1-fy-2025-26/); [Lenovo Q2 FY2025/26](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/q2-fy-2025-26/); [Lenovo Q3 FY2025/26](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/q3-fy-2025-26/); [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

That progression materially changed Lenovo's earnings mix. The 2014 IBM x86 and Motorola transactions had always been framed as diversification away from pure PC cyclicality. Motorola never delivered the same economic logic. The x86 server business eventually did. A decade after the acquisition, the unit had become the company's clearest AI infrastructure lever and, by FY2026, its first new large business in years to reach full-year profitability. [IBM x86 closing](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/lenovo-set-to-close-acquisition-ibms-x86-server-business/); [Motorola closing](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/lenovo-completes-full-acquisition-motorola-mobility-from-google/); [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

| Metric | FY2022 | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | FY2026 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Group revenue (US$bn) | 71.6 | 61.9 | 56.9 | 69.1 | 83.1 |
| Year-on-year change | +21% | -13% | -8% | +21% | +20% |
| ISG operating status | Loss | Loss | Loss | Broke even in 2H | Full-year profit |

## The FY2026 landing

By the time Lenovo reported FY2025/26 on May 22 2026, the language had changed from recovery to expansion. The company described FY2025/26 as the strongest year in its history; group revenue exceeded US$80 billion for the first time; adjusted net income rose 42 per cent to US$2.0 billion; and AI-related revenue grew 105 per cent to account for 33 per cent of the total. IDG contributed US$58.9 billion of annual revenue, SSG surpassed US$10 billion, and ISG achieved the profitability target that had eluded it for years. [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

## Two decades, two pivots

Yang Yuanqing's tenure gave Lenovo unusual continuity across both of its defining pivots. The first was the IBM PC transaction, announced in December 2004 and closed in May 2005, which turned a Chinese domestic manufacturer into a global commercial-PC brand. The second was the 2014 server acquisition, which only became fully legible in the financials a decade later as AI infrastructure demand rose. [IBM PC acquisition](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/lenovo-to-acquire-ibm-personal-computing-division/); [IBM x86 closing](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/lenovo-set-to-close-acquisition-ibms-x86-server-business/)

The corrected earnings story, then, was not that Lenovo had flattened out at roughly US$57 billion of annual revenue and was waiting for the next cycle. It was that the company had already come off the bottom, recovered its FY2025 scale, and then exceeded its old peak in FY2026 on the back of a materially different mix of profits and growth drivers. That distinction mattered to any serious reading of the dossier. [Five-Year Financial Summary](https://investor.lenovo.com/en/financial/five_year_summary.php); [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

chapters.title: Yang Yuanqing, segment presidents, and the board
chapters.body:
## The executive who became the continuity trade

Few global hardware groups of Lenovo's scale had been defined by one operating leader for as long as Lenovo had been defined by Yang Yuanqing. He joined the group in 1989, became an executive director in 1997, was chairman from April 30 2005, resumed the chief executive role on February 5 2009, and by the frozen snapshot date still held both titles. The chronology mattered because it corrected one of the earlier draft's central mistakes: Yang had not been continuously chairman and chief executive since 2004, but he had been the company's dominant operating figure for more than two decades. [Our Leadership](https://www.lenovo.com/us/en/about/who-we-are/our-leadership/index.html); [Board of Directors](https://investor.lenovo.com/en/cg/directors.php)

By May 2026 he sat atop the strongest financial year in Lenovo's history. FY2025/26 revenue reached US$83.1 billion, adjusted net income rose 42 per cent to US$2.0 billion, and the company used the release to say it was confident in becoming a US$100 billion company within two years. That ambition was not background colour; it framed the governance question around Yang's long tenure. [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

## Founder succession

Liu Chuanzhi remained essential to the company's identity but no longer to day-to-day control. Legend Holdings, Lenovo's controlling shareholder, described Liu as founder of both Legend Holdings and Lenovo Group and as its honorary chairman. Lenovo's ownership chain still therefore carried his institutional imprint even after he retired from active leadership. [Legend founder page](https://www.legendholdings.com.cn/common_en/index.aspx?nodeid=1122); [Legend company introduction](https://www.legendholdings.com.cn/Introduction_en/index.aspx?nodeid=1043)

## A three-segment architecture, three operating presidents

Under Yang, Lenovo's structure had become more explicit. Luca Rossi, who joined Lenovo in 2015, served as executive vice president and president of IDG, overseeing PCs, smartphones, tablets, workstations, software and collaboration products. Ken Wong served as executive vice president and president of SSG; Lenovo's leadership page said he had previously led Asia Pacific PCs and Smart Devices for five years, chaired NEC Lenovo Japan Group from 2016 to early 2021, and chaired Fujitsu Client Computing from 2018 to early 2021. [Our Leadership](https://www.lenovo.com/us/en/about/who-we-are/our-leadership/index.html)

Wong's unit had grown into a larger and better-defined business than the earlier dossier suggested. In Q1 FY2025/26 Lenovo said SSG revenue rose 20 per cent year on year to US$2.3 billion and that managed services, as-a-service offerings, projects and solutions accounted for 58 per cent of segment revenue. By Q4 FY2025/26 revenue had reached US$2.6 billion, fourth-quarter operating margin stood at 22.4 per cent, and Managed Services plus Project and Solutions mix had risen to 62 per cent. [Lenovo Q1 FY2025/26](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/q1-fy-2025-26/); [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

## ISG: the most consequential chair, and the hardest to fill

The most sensitive leadership transition sat in ISG. Lenovo said on June 6 2024 that Kirk Skaugen, head of ISG, would leave the company effective immediately and that Greg Huff and Vlad Rozanovich would jointly lead the business on an interim basis. On October 23 2024 Lenovo then announced that Ashley Gorakhpurwalla would join on November 11 as executive vice president and president of ISG. The company described him as the former president and general manager of Servers and Infrastructure Systems at Dell EMC and, more recently, executive vice president and general manager of HDD at Western Digital. [Statement on Kirk Skaugen](https://news.lenovo.com/?p=28346); [Ashley Gorakhpurwalla appointment](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/ashley-gorakhpurwalla-joins-lenovo/); [Our Leadership](https://www.lenovo.com/us/en/about/who-we-are/our-leadership/index.html)

The timing proved consequential. Under Gorakhpurwalla's first full months in seat, ISG moved from a business that had only broken even in the second half of FY2024/25 to one that reached full-year profitability in FY2025/26. Revenue rose from US$14.5 billion in FY2024/25 to US$19.2 billion in FY2025/26; fourth-quarter operating profit reached US$202 million; annual manufacturing capacity surpassed 70,000 racks; and customer AI deployments exceeded 5,800. What had previously been presented as a turnaround plan started to look like an executed one. [Lenovo FY2024/25 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2024-25/); [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

## The board: control, memory, and international signalling

Lenovo's board also looked different once the non-primary ownership citation was removed. As of the board page available within the frozen window, Lenovo had eleven directors: one executive director, four non-executive directors, and six independent non-executive directors. As of March 31 2025, Lenovo's own shareholding page showed Legend Holdings owned 31.41 per cent of the shares, Yang 5.94 per cent, and other directors 0.11 per cent. [Board of Directors](https://investor.lenovo.com/en/cg/directors.php); [Shareholding Structure](https://investor.lenovo.com/en/ir/shareholding.php)

The non-executive layer linked the operating company back to the shareholder structure. Zhu Linan had been a non-executive director since 2005 and had previously served as president of Legend Holdings. Zhao John Huan, on Lenovo's board since 2011, had also been re-designated as a non-executive director of Legend Holdings effective January 1 2020. Wong Wai Ming moved into a non-executive seat on April 1 2025 after more than 17 years as group chief financial officer. Laura Green Quatela made the same move after retiring as chief legal and corporate responsibility officer at March 31 2025. [Board of Directors](https://investor.lenovo.com/en/cg/directors.php)

The independent slate was more international than the old ownership summary implied. John Lawson Thornton became lead independent director on February 21 2025; Gordon Orr brought a McKinsey-and-Asia technology background; Kasper Bo Roersted joined in February 2024 after leading adidas and Henkel; Woo Chin Wan Raymond was a retired Ernst & Young partner; Yang Lan remained one of the group's most recognisable Chinese public-facing independents; Cher Wang brought HTC and VIA credentials; and Professor Xue Lan added an AI-governance and public-policy profile from Tsinghua. [Board of Directors](https://investor.lenovo.com/en/cg/directors.php)

## The governance question

The question Yang's tenure posed did not disappear simply because the operating record improved. Lenovo was still a company with a combined chairman-chief executive, a controlling shareholder that traced its own founding to the Institute of Computing Technology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, and a business increasingly exposed to AI infrastructure, public-policy scrutiny and cross-border capital allocation. But the facts had to be stated accurately: the ownership stake was 31.41 per cent, not roughly 29 per cent; the current title chronology was more complex than a simple "since 2004"; and the strongest case for governance continuity was that the structure had, at least through May 23 2026, produced the best financial year in Lenovo's history. [Shareholding Structure](https://investor.lenovo.com/en/ir/shareholding.php); [Legend company introduction](https://www.legendholdings.com.cn/Introduction_en/index.aspx?nodeid=1043); [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

chapters.title: PC customers, hyperscaler AI server, enterprise IT, and the manufacturing footprint
chapters.body:
## The world's biggest PC franchise

Lenovo still approached the market from the top of the PC volume table. By FY2025/26 it described itself as serving customers in 180 markets, and the year-end release showed IDG revenue of US$58.9 billion, up 17 per cent year on year. ThinkPad remained the flagship commercial brand, but the installed base had broadened to include ThinkBook, Yoga, Legion, tablets, workstations and Motorola smartphones. The important point for this chapter was not branding alone; it was that Lenovo's customer relationships remained broad enough to seed both services attachment and infrastructure cross-sell. [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

Large enterprise fleets still anchored the model. The commercial refresh story that appeared in FY2025/26 results was tied to AI PCs, premium mix and share gains rather than to a return to the old pandemic surge. In the fourth quarter, global PC market share reached 24.4 per cent and premium-PC mix reached 50 per cent. That gave Lenovo a larger installed base through which to sell support, managed devices and eventually AI infrastructure. [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

## Hyperscaler AI server demand

The more consequential customer shift sat inside ISG. Lenovo did not name its largest hyperscaler accounts in the FY2025/26 disclosures reviewed through the frozen window, but it disclosed enough to show the scale of demand: a US$21 billion AI-server pipeline, more than 5,800 customer AI deployments, and quarterly ISG revenue that rose to US$5.6 billion in Q4. Earlier quarterly releases showed the build-up: Q1 ISG revenue of US$4.3 billion, Q2 of US$4.1 billion, and Q3 of US$5.2 billion. [Lenovo Q1 FY2025/26](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/q1-fy-2025-26/); [Lenovo Q2 FY2025/26](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/q2-fy-2025-26/); [Lenovo Q3 FY2025/26](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/q3-fy-2025-26/); [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

The disclosures were also more specific on product direction than the draft suggested. Lenovo said the rack-scale roadmap had advanced to first shipments of GB300 NVL72 racks in the last quarter of FY2025/26, with Rubin-based platforms on track for the second half. That mattered because it showed ISG serving not just conventional enterprise refresh but the highest-density end of the AI infrastructure market. [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

## Enterprise IT: breadth over concentration

Below the hyperscaler tier, Lenovo kept addressing a wider enterprise customer set: private-cloud buyers using ThinkAgile, mid-market and enterprise accounts buying conventional x86 refreshes, and customers consuming infrastructure through TruScale or project-based SSG engagements. The group's disclosures repeatedly framed that model as one that stretched "from pocket to cloud" and from edge to data centre, with SSG providing the higher-value services layer around hardware deployments. [Lenovo FY2024/25 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2024-25/); [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

What the company did not do, even after the May 2026 full-year results, was name major hyperscaler or regulated-enterprise contracts individually. Where the earlier draft had left that point hanging, the primary-source answer was simpler: Lenovo chose commercial confidentiality over account-level disclosure, while still reporting the pipeline, deployment count and rack capacity needed for investors to infer scale. [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

## Manufacturing: the geo-balanced model

Lenovo's own wording on manufacturing was more concrete than the draft's speculation. The FY2025/26 results release said the company had a global supply chain with **more than 30 manufacturing sites across 10 markets**. The route to that footprint had been laid out across company releases over time: in 2007 Lenovo announced new manufacturing plants in Monterrey, Mexico and Baddi, India; in 2020 it said its new in-house site in Ullo, Hungary would make desktops, workstations and data-centre products; and in North Carolina it opened a US PC manufacturing line in Whitsett in 2013. [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/); [Mexico and India expansion](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/lenovo-to-increase-global-footprint-with-new-manufacturing-plants-in-mexico-and-india/); [Hungary manufacturing facility](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/lenovo-expands-global-manufacturing-portfolio-with-new-inhouse-manufacturing-facility-in-hungary/); [Whitsett opening](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/lenovo-announces-official-opening-of-u-s-computer-manufacturing-line-in-north-carolina/)

The Whitsett point mattered because the old dossier misidentified the site as a server plant. Lenovo's own US manufacturing announcements described Whitsett as a **computer** manufacturing line capable of producing products such as the ThinkCentre M92p Tiny desktop and ThinkPad Tablet 2. That did not make the site strategically unimportant. It did mean the chapter needed to state its function accurately. [US manufacturing line announcement](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/lenovo-to-open-computer-manufacturing-line-in-the-united-states/); [Whitsett opening](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/lenovo-announces-official-opening-of-u-s-computer-manufacturing-line-in-north-carolina/)

Hungary was the cleaner example of a direct link between geography and product mix. Lenovo said the Ullo site would produce desktops, workstations and data-centre products for Europe, explicitly tying location to delivery times and manufacturing-network optimisation. That was the kind of primary-source evidence the earlier draft had gestured toward without pinning down. [Hungary manufacturing facility](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/lenovo-expands-global-manufacturing-portfolio-with-new-inhouse-manufacturing-facility-in-hungary/)

## Geopolitical exposure and tariff architecture

The tariff discussion also needed a tighter factual base. Management did not break out a stand-alone tariff charge in the FY2025/26 disclosures reviewed through the frozen window. What it did say was that Lenovo had navigated tariff volatility through a resilient supply chain, a balanced sales footprint, its ODM+ model and its global-local operating structure. In the August 2025 Q1 release, Yang said Lenovo had "overcame challenges brought by tariff volatility and the geopolitical landscape"; in the May 2026 full-year release, the company again pointed to structural resilience in a volatile environment marked by supply shortages, rising component costs and broader uncertainty. [Lenovo Q1 FY2025/26](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/q1-fy-2025-26/); [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

That did not eliminate geopolitical risk. It did answer the draft's research gap more honestly. Through May 23 2026 Lenovo disclosed the tools it said it was using to offset tariff pressure, but it did not publish a discrete quantified tariff hit or a facility-by-facility transfer schedule. The right sourced conclusion was therefore narrower than the old one: Lenovo had diversified footprint and management said it was working, but the exact offset value remained undisclosed in primary company filings. [Lenovo Q1 FY2025/26](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/q1-fy-2025-26/); [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

chapters.title: Where Lenovo sits against Dell, HPE, SMCI in servers, plus PC competitive set
chapters.body:
## A Company Competing on Several Fronts

By May 2026 Lenovo was competing from two very different starting positions. In personal computers it remained the scale leader; in infrastructure it had only just turned a decade-old acquisition into a profitable AI-server business. The same FY2025/26 release that recorded a record 24.4 per cent fourth-quarter PC market share also showed ISG revenue of US$19.2 billion and full-year operating profit of US$73 million. The competitive question was therefore no longer whether Lenovo had size. It was whether that size could be defended in devices while margins widened in infrastructure and services. [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

## PCs: leadership by disclosed share rather than tracker estimates

Lenovo's own disclosures gave the cleanest measure of its device position inside the frozen window. In the fourth quarter of FY2025/26, the company said global PC market share reached a record 24.4 per cent, leaving a 2.8-point gap to the second-ranked vendor. Premium-PC mix reached 50 per cent, and AI-PC shipments rose to 4.5 million units, representing more than 20 per cent of Lenovo notebook shipments worldwide. That supported a narrower but better-sourced conclusion than the draft's third-party market-share table: Lenovo entered FY2027 as the volume leader with improving mix and a visible AI-device ramp. [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

The nearest competitive comparisons remained HP Inc and Dell in commercial Windows fleets, and Apple in premium notebooks. Lenovo's reviewed primary disclosures did not publish peers' exact unit shares, and the dossier did not need to infer them. What mattered was the pattern visible in Lenovo's own numbers: commercial refresh, premium mix and AI-capable devices had improved together. The company's claim to defensibility rested less on any single form factor than on breadth across ThinkPad, ThinkBook, Yoga, Legion and Motorola, combined with a distribution and supply-chain network that management said spanned 180 markets. [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

That breadth also set the limits of the comparison. Apple still competed for the premium end of the notebook market, while HP and Dell remained entrenched in enterprise procurement. Lenovo's advantage, as disclosed by the company itself, was that it had entered the AI-PC cycle from a position of already-record share rather than from a need to regain it. [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

## The Server Market: Dell ahead, Lenovo now credible

The infrastructure comparison changed more materially once the figures were checked against primary sources. Through the frozen window, Lenovo had already moved well past the subscale revenue base implied in the draft: FY2025/26 ISG revenue was US$19.2 billion. That still left Dell ahead by a wide margin and kept HPE and Supermicro relevant benchmarks, but it placed Lenovo firmly inside the first tier of global infrastructure vendors rather than at its edge. [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

| Vendor | Latest primary-source revenue base before 2026-05-23 | AI-server emphasis | Key differentiator |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dell Technologies | ISG FY2026 revenue US$60.8B | AI-optimized servers, bespoke clusters | Scale, enterprise direct sales, global support |
| HPE | Server FY2025 revenue US$17.7B | ProLiant AI systems, GreenLake attach | Enterprise installed base, consumption model |
| Supermicro | FY2025 net sales US$22.0B | AI platforms, liquid cooling | Speed to market, AI-specialist focus |
| Lenovo | ISG FY2026 revenue US$19.2B | ThinkSystem, ThinkAgile, Neptune, rack-scale AI | Global-local supply chain, Asia and enterprise breadth |

[Dell FY2026 results](https://investors.delltechnologies.com/news-releases/news-release-details/dell-technologies-delivers-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-fiscal-3); [HPE FY2025 results](https://investors.hpe.com/~/media/Files/H/HP-Enterprise-IR/documents/q4-2025/q4-2025-earnings-press-release.pdf); [Supermicro FY2025 results](https://ir.supermicro.com/news/news-details/2025/Supermicro-Announces-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Fiscal-Year-2025-Financial-Results/default.aspx); [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

Dell's advantage remained structural rather than merely technological. Its FY2026 results showed US$60.8 billion of ISG revenue and US$24.7 billion of annual AI-optimized server revenue, evidence of a direct-sales and deployment machine that Lenovo had not matched in depth outside selected markets. HPE's comparison point was reported differently, but its fiscal-2025 disclosures still showed US$17.7 billion of server revenue and a more established enterprise consumption framework. Supermicro's FY2025 results showed US$22.0 billion of net sales, confirming that an AI-specialist vendor could scale into Lenovo's neighbourhood very quickly when speed to market mattered most. [Dell FY2026 results](https://investors.delltechnologies.com/news-releases/news-release-details/dell-technologies-delivers-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-fiscal-3); [HPE FY2025 results](https://investors.hpe.com/~/media/Files/H/HP-Enterprise-IR/documents/q4-2025/q4-2025-earnings-press-release.pdf); [Supermicro FY2025 results](https://ir.supermicro.com/news/news-details/2025/Supermicro-Announces-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Fiscal-Year-2025-Financial-Results/default.aspx)

Lenovo's counter-argument was that it had become both broader and more credible. Its FY2025/26 disclosures showed full-year ISG profitability, a US$21 billion AI-server pipeline, more than 5,800 customer AI deployments, and annual manufacturing capacity above 70,000 racks, including more than 11,000 direct-liquid-cooled racks. That did not erase the gap with Dell, but it did change the competitive conversation from whether Lenovo belonged in AI infrastructure to whether it could deepen margins while remaining in the front rank. [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

## The hyperscaler problem and the ODM+ response

The structural threat beneath all branded infrastructure vendors remained direct hyperscaler procurement. Lenovo's own disclosures did not name every competing original-design manufacturer, but they made clear that cloud service provider demand was becoming more important. In the Q3 FY2025/26 release, management highlighted record CSP revenue, and by year-end the company was describing a larger AI-server pipeline and first shipments of GB300 NVL72 racks. That was the factual basis for the ODM+ discussion: Lenovo was trying to serve both the traditional enterprise channel and the more customised, lower-margin, hyperscaler-style deployment model. [Lenovo Q3 FY2025/26](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/q3-fy-2025-26/); [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

That response carried a trade-off. The deeper Lenovo moved into highly customised AI racks, the harder it became to rely only on the historical OEM model of standard systems sold through broad channels at stable gross margins. The attraction was volume and relevance; the risk was that absolute revenue would grow faster than returns.

## SSG: services as the competitive glue

The third competitive dimension was SSG, where Lenovo positioned against both IT-services providers and OEMs trying to build annuity layers around infrastructure. HPE's GreenLake remained the clearest comparable model. Lenovo's own FY2025/26 disclosures showed SSG annual revenue surpassing US$10 billion, fourth-quarter operating margin at 22.4 per cent, and Managed Services plus Project and Solutions mix at 62 per cent of quarterly revenue. The competitive argument was that this services wrapper could make Lenovo harder to dislodge in both device and infrastructure accounts. [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/); [HPE FY2025 results](https://investors.hpe.com/~/media/Files/H/HP-Enterprise-IR/documents/q4-2025/q4-2025-earnings-press-release.pdf)

By the frozen date, that thesis was still being executed rather than proved beyond doubt. But it was materially better supported than the earlier draft had allowed. Lenovo no longer competed only as a PC vendor trying to branch into servers. It competed as a scale device company, a newly profitable AI-infrastructure supplier and a growing services provider, each helping to defend the others. [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

chapters.title: From 1984 founding through IBM acquisitions and ISG inflection
chapters.body:
## Catalysts at a Glance

This chapter identifies the forward variables that were already visible in primary company disclosures by the frozen-window date of May 23 2026. For the historical timeline — the 1984 founding, the 2005 IBM PC acquisition, and the 2014 System x and Motorola transactions — see the Corporate History chapter.

## AI PCs and the premium-mix upgrade

The first catalyst sat inside IDG. Lenovo's FY2025/26 results showed fourth-quarter global PC market share at a record 24.4 per cent, a 2.8-point lead over the nearest competitor, premium-PC mix at 50 per cent, and AI-PC shipments of 4.5 million units, representing more than 20 per cent of Lenovo notebook shipments worldwide. That combination mattered because it suggested the PC recovery was no longer purely cyclical volume restoration; it was also becoming a mix and feature-cycle story tied to AI-capable devices. [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

## ISG's disclosed AI-server pipeline

The second catalyst was the one the market had started valuing most aggressively: AI infrastructure. Lenovo's May 2026 full-year release disclosed a US$21 billion AI-server pipeline, more than 5,800 customer AI deployments, annual manufacturing capacity above 70,000 racks, and more than 11,000 direct-liquid-cooled racks built for AI workloads. The same release said first GB300 NVL72 shipments had already started in the last quarter of FY2025/26, with Rubin-based platforms expected in the second half. That left the next reporting periods exposed not to a hypothetical product roadmap but to conversion, margin and fulfilment questions around a pipeline the company had already quantified. [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

## SSG and recurring-revenue mix

The third catalyst remained SSG, which had become the clearest margin lever in Lenovo's model. FY2025/26 took annual SSG revenue above US$10 billion for the first time; in the fourth quarter the segment posted 22.4 per cent operating margin, while Managed Services plus Project and Solutions accounted for 62 per cent of quarterly revenue. Earlier in the year, Lenovo had already told investors that the faster-growing managed-services, as-a-service, projects and solutions categories had reached 58 per cent of SSG revenue in Q1. The signal was consistent across the year: the services layer was becoming larger and more recurring. [Lenovo Q1 FY2025/26](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/q1-fy-2025-26/); [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

## The strategic thread

The thread connecting all three catalysts was the same one Yang Yuanqing had articulated for years, but the frozen-window evidence behind it was stronger by May 2026 than it had been a year earlier. IDG still supplied the installed base, ISG had become a profitable AI-infrastructure engine, and SSG was extracting a growing share of higher-margin recurring revenue from both. The next phase of the Lenovo story therefore depended less on proving that these pieces belonged together than on proving that the economics would continue to improve once the first wave of AI spending normalised. [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

chapters.title: ThinkPad heritage, server IP, R&D framework
chapters.body:
## The Yamato Inheritance

When Lenovo's engineers flew to Tokyo's western suburbs in 2005 to take possession of IBM's ThinkPad operation, they were acquiring something more valuable than a product line. The Yamato Laboratory in Kanagawa prefecture — where Arimasa Naitoh and a generation of engineers had defined portable computing aesthetics since the first black-lidded ThinkPad shipped in 1992 — came with the deal intact. IBM had preserved Yamato as the nerve centre of ThinkPad design; Lenovo preserved it again.

The decision to keep Yamato operational rather than fold it into Chinese engineering operations signalled a deliberate IP custodianship strategy. Richard Sapper's original industrial design language — the matte-black rectilinear chassis, the angular lid, the red TrackPoint pointing nub centred above the B-key — had accumulated brand equity that no rebadging exercise could replicate. Lenovo's management understood that the design conventions *were* the intellectual property, as much as any specific patent claim.

The 2005 transaction transferred the ThinkPad and ThinkCentre brands, associated tooling and manufacturing know-how, and a patent estate covering keyboard mechanisms, thermal management architectures, and display-hinge engineering accumulated over thirteen years of IBM PC development. Lenovo simultaneously secured a licence to the broader IBM portfolio for five years, providing a runway to build out its own independent filing programme.

## From System x to ThinkSystem

The 2014 IBM x86 server acquisition delivered a second and structurally distinct IP tranche. IBM's System x product family — rack-mount servers, BladeCenter blade systems, Flex System converged infrastructure, and the NeXtScale high-density compute platform — came with engineering teams in Research Triangle Park, North Carolina, and a patent estate concentrated in server thermal engineering, blade interconnect architectures, and systems-management firmware.

Under Lenovo stewardship, System x was rebranded ThinkSystem for mainstream rack and tower configurations and ThinkAgile for hyperconverged infrastructure stacks. The nomenclature continuity with ThinkPad was deliberate: the "Think" prefix had become a quality signal in commercial IT procurement, and extending it to server iron transferred brand equity accumulated over two decades of notebook sales into a category where Lenovo was still a new entrant.

The organic ISG engineering that followed the acquisition added materially to this foundation. Lenovo's teams in Morrisville, North Carolina — retained wholesale from the IBM transaction — developed next-generation server platform designs including the Neptune direct liquid-cooling architecture, which became central to the company's pitch to hyperscaler customers deploying GPU-dense AI inference and training clusters. Neptune's direct water-cooling and warm-water immersion implementations, engineered to handle the thermal envelopes of NVIDIA H-series and AMD Instinct accelerators, represented genuinely novel systems engineering developed post-acquisition rather than inherited from IBM — the clearest example of Lenovo building on an IP foundation rather than merely maintaining one.

## Patent Portfolio

The earlier draft's patent paragraph was too impressionistic. Lenovo did not publish a single consolidated patent total in the primary company materials reviewed through the frozen window, but the record was far less opaque than that sentence implied. In 2014 Lenovo said it had bought **more than 3,800 patent families** from NEC Corporation, while the Motorola Mobility acquisition transferred **more than 2,000 patent assets** together with the Motorola trademark portfolio and a licence to Google's retained patent estate. The board biography of Laura Green Quatela also showed that global legal and IP management remained a named executive responsibility inside Lenovo through March 2025. [NEC patent acquisition](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/lenovo-to-buy-mobile-patents-from-nec-corporation/); [Motorola acquisition](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/lenovo-to-acquire-motorola-mobility-from-google/); [Motorola closing](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/lenovo-completes-full-acquisition-motorola-mobility-from-google/); [Board of Directors](https://investor.lenovo.com/en/cg/directors.php)

That picture better matched the commercial reality. Lenovo's mobile and PC portfolio carried meaningful standards and trademark exposure because of Motorola, ThinkPad and related wireless assets, while the server portfolio skewed more heavily toward implementation IP in cooling, systems management and chassis engineering. The company's public disputes with Ericsson over standard-essential patents underscored that Lenovo remained an active participant in licensing and rate-setting battles rather than a passive buyer of old portfolios. [Lenovo on Ericsson litigation](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/lenovo-statement-on-the-us-international-trade-commission-ruling/)
## R&D Framework

Lenovo's R&D description also needed to be updated to the latest disclosed footprint. In its FY2025/26 full-year release, the company said it had **21 research and development locations in 11 markets**. The old draft's reference to seven principal sites therefore understated the disclosed scale, even if Yamato, Morrisville, Beijing and selected European centres still carried disproportionate weight in practice. [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

The spending line had risen with the AI build-out. Lenovo said R&D expense increased 13 per cent year on year to US$2.3 billion in FY2024/25, then rose a further 9 per cent in FY2025/26 to around 3 per cent of group revenue. The company framed that investment as part of its effort to build a hybrid-AI stack spanning devices, infrastructure, software, solutions and services. [Lenovo FY2024/25 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2024-25/); [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

The ThinkPad lineage still provided the template for what Lenovo appeared to be trying to do in servers. It preserved Yamato as an engineering signal, kept extending the "Think" brand into ThinkSystem and ThinkAgile, and used internally developed Neptune liquid cooling as proof that the post-IBM server business was adding fresh engineering rather than merely monetising inherited assets. The question the market still had to answer was whether that engineering identity would translate into durable pricing power. Through May 2026, the evidence had become stronger, but it was not yet definitive. [Lenovo history](https://www.lenovo.com/us/en/about/who-we-are/history/); [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

chapters.title: US-China geopolitical, PC cycle, ISG competitive intensity, governance
chapters.body:
## US-China Trade and Policy Exposure

No risk sat closer to Lenovo's corporate structure than the US-China policy divide. The company still combined Beijing and Morrisville operating centres, remained listed in Hong Kong, and sold products that depended on US, Taiwanese, Korean and Chinese technology supply chains at the same time. Through the frozen window, Lenovo's public disclosures described resilience rather than immunity: management repeatedly pointed to a global-local operating model, a balanced geographic footprint and a supply chain spread across more than 30 sites in 10 markets. [Corporate Information](https://investor.lenovo.com/en/about/corpinfo.php); [Lenovo Q1 FY2025/26](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/q1-fy-2025-26/); [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

The most direct channel of policy risk remained advanced semiconductors. ISG's AI-server push depended heavily on Nvidia GPUs and related memory, networking and cooling systems. That meant US export-control policy could affect what Lenovo sold, where it sold it, and how quickly it fulfilled AI infrastructure orders. The company did not disclose a quantified export-control revenue drag in the releases reviewed through May 23 2026, but the dependency itself was plain from the product and pipeline disclosures. [Lenovo Q3 FY2025/26](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/q3-fy-2025-26/); [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

## PC Cycle Exposure

The draft's biggest risk-section error was temporal. Revenue did not stabilise at roughly US$57 billion in FY2025. It fell from US$71.6 billion in FY2022 to US$56.9 billion in FY2024, then recovered to US$69.1 billion in FY2025 and US$83.1 billion in FY2026. That correction mattered analytically because the risk question had shifted. The issue was no longer whether Lenovo could survive a post-Covid drawdown; it was whether AI-PC demand and enterprise refresh could remain durable enough to prevent another air pocket once the initial rebound ran its course. [Five-Year Financial Summary](https://investor.lenovo.com/en/financial/five_year_summary.php); [Lenovo FY2024/25 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2024-25/); [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

The evidence was encouraging but not conclusive. Lenovo said AI-PC penetration accelerated in FY2025/26, fourth-quarter PC market share reached 24.4 per cent, and premium-PC mix reached 50 per cent. Those were useful indicators of quality of recovery. They did not prove that demand would remain immune to macro slowdown or that premium pricing would hold once AI-PC offerings became standard across the industry. [Lenovo Q1 FY2025/26](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/q1-fy-2025-26/); [Lenovo FY2025/26 results](https://news.lenovo.com/pressroom/press-releases/fy-2025-26/)

## ISG Competitive Intensity

The AI-server business remained the central growth narrative, and therefore the central execution risk. Lenovo exited FY2025/26 with US$19.2 billion of ISG revenue, a US$21 billion AI-server pipeline and full-year profitability. But the competitive field remained heavy.
